steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Do hidden states in large language models (LLMs) encode tokens that are farther than one token ahead? And if they do, how can we decode this sequence of tokens from just one state? In this work we investigate these questions empirically, using GPT-J-6B. We train models that predict hidden states several tokens ahead of a position t, using only the contextualized representation of the input at that position.

Auto-regressive transformer language models are usually trained to predict one token ahead. But recent work has hinted that individual hidden states may have more information in them than only the probabilities of the next token. For example, Meng et al. trace how information flows from subject tokens to associated attribute predictions many steps ahead. Gurnee et al. suggest that neurons in early layers are dense with information, and that middle layers have dedicated neurons which represent high-level contextual features.

  - pass intermediate hidden states directly to decoder head, skipping in-between layers, to "verbalize" embeddings
  - memorization studies: very long memorized sequences generated by LMs
  - progressively dropping layers still gives similar prediction output vs. fully computed run

  - 1: extend Tuned Lens and Logit lens; linear models approximating future predictions several tokens ahead
  - 2: causal intervention; transplant hidden states into a completely different context; measure if originally predicted future tokens are still predicted
  - 3: fit a "soft prompt" to read out subsequent-token info from a hidden state

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Do hidden states in large language models (LLMs) encode tokens that are farther than one token ahead? And if they do, how can we decode this sequence of tokens from just one state? In this work we investigate these questions empirically, using GPT-J-6B. We train models that predict hidden states several tokens ahead of a position t, using only the contextualized representation of the input at that position.

Auto-regressive transformer language models are usually trained to predict one token ahead. But recent work has hinted that individual hidden states may have more information in them than only the probabilities of the next token. For example, Meng et al. trace how information flows from subject tokens to associated attribute predictions many steps ahead. Gurnee et al. suggest that neurons in early layers are dense with information, and that middle layers have dedicated neurons which represent high-level contextual features.

Other work has passed intermediate hidden states directly to the decoder head, skipping the layers in between, to "verbalize" such embeddings. Studies of memorization have found that language models generate very long memorized sequences. Also, prior work shows that if you progressively drop layers during computation, you can still get a similar prediction output to the model when you compare it to the fully computed model run.

So in this work we ask: how much information about future (beyond subsequent) tokens can we extract from a single hidden token representation? We do three experiments to answer this. First, we extend the ideas of Tuned Lens and the Logit lens and train linear models that approximate the model's future predictions several tokens in the future, to show how much individual hidden states may directly encode subsequent tokens. Second, we do a causal intervention study where we transplant individual hidden states from one context into a completely different context, and we measure how much the future tokens that were predicted in the original context can be predicted in the foreign context. Finally, we fit a "soft prompt" that explicitly learns an optimal prompt for reading out information about subsequent tokens from a hidden state. Our code and data is available at https://future.baulab.info

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Do hidden states in large language models (LLMs) encode tokens farther than a single token ahead? If so, how can we decode this sequence of tokens from a single state? In this work we empirically investigate these questions using GPT-J-6B [1]. We train models to predict hidden states several tokens ahead of a given position t, based only on the contextualized representation of the input at that position.

Auto-regressive transformer language models are typically trained to predict one token ahead, but recent work has hinted that individual hidden states may contain more information than just the probabilities of the following token. For example, Meng et al. [2] trace information flow from subject tokens to associated attribute predictions many steps ahead. Elsewhere, Gurnee et al. [3] suggest that neurons in early layers are dense with information, while middle layers have dedicated neurons representing high-level contextual features.

Other related efforts have passed intermediate hidden states directly to the decoder head (skipping the in-between layers) to "verbalize" such embeddings [4,5,6]. Studies of memorization [7,8,9] have identified very long memorized sequences generated by language models, and [10] shows that progressively dropping layers during computation can still achieve a prediction output similar to that of the fully computed model run.

In this work we ask: To what extent can we extract information about future (beyond subsequent) tokens from a single hidden token representation? To answer this, we conduct three experiments. First, extending the ideas of Tuned Lens [5,4] and the Logit lens [6], we train linear models to approximate future model predictions several tokens in the future, to reveal the extent to which individual hidden states may directly encode subsequent tokens. Second, we perform a causal intervention study in which we transplant individual hidden states from one context to a completely different context and measure how far future tokens predicted in the original context can still be predicted in the foreign context. Finally, we fit a "soft prompt" that explicitly learns an optimal prompt for reading out information about subsequent tokens from a hidden state. Our code and data is available at https://future.baulab.info
